title: Why did Britain skip 11 days in 1752?

sources.name: UK legislation — Calendar (New Style) Act 1750, sections 1–2
Royal Museums Greenwich — Leap years and the 1752 calendar change

practice: Try the History Quiz for more questions about how we describe the past.

sections.title: Why did the date jump from 2 to 14 September?
sections.html:
Britain skipped eleven date labels in September 1752 when it changed from the Julian calendar to the Gregorian calendar. The calendars had drifted eleven days apart.

Go to bed on 2 September; wake up on 14 September. Only one ordinary night had passed. Your diary needed a surprising new heading, not eleven missing entries.

sections.title: Two calendars had stopped agreeing
sections.html:
The calendars used different leap-year rules. Over time, those small differences added up. Skipping dates brought Britain into line with the Gregorian calendar.

Royal Museums Greenwich records the switch. The new rules still matter today: they explain why 2100 will not have a leap day.

sections.title: Which eleven dates were left out?
sections.html:
3–13 September 1752, inclusive. The count is 13 − 3 + 1 = 11. The next date after 2 September was therefore 14 September.

It is like changing the number on the next notebook page. The label jumps, but no extra pages have been read.

sections.title: Other countries changed at other times
sections.html:
This was not a worldwide switch on one morning. For a historical date, check where it was recorded and which calendar was in use.

And if a century label causes the next puzzle, 1900 and 1901 make a useful comparison.

description: Britain jumped from 2 to 14 September 1752 to bring its calendar into line. Here is why eleven date labels vanished, while ordinary days kept passing.
